items.en: Tomorrow I will study in the library.
He will write us a letter.
She will finish the work in the evening.
We will listen to music in the car.
They will study at the university.
When will you close the shop? (to a man)
I'll save you a seat.
Next year we will finish our studies.

lessons.title: Will Go, Will Come, Will Be

items.en: Tomorrow I'll go to the doctor.
She will come at eight.
It will be fine.
What will we do on Shabbat?
I will be at home all day.
They will go to the beach in the morning.
Tomorrow it will be hot.
We'll come to you in the evening.
Come here, please. (to a man)
Come on, let's go. (to a woman)
Sit down, please. (to a man)
Give me the key. (to a man)
Don't worry. (to a man)
Don't forget the phone. (to a woman)
Tell me when. (to a man)
Come and eat! (to everyone)

items.he: אֲנִי לֹא בָּא כִּי אֲנִי חוֹלֶה.
items.en: I'm not coming because I'm sick.
items.translit: Ani lo ba ki ani chole.

items.en: When I'm tired, I drink coffee.
If it's hot, we'll go to the beach.

items.he: רָצִיתִי לָבוֹא, אֲבָל לֹא הָיָה לִי זְמַן.
items.en: I wanted to come, but I didn't have time.
items.translit: Ratsiti lavo, aval lo haya li zman.

items.en: It rained, so we stayed home.
If you want, we can meet tomorrow.
When I was a child, we lived in Haifa.

items.he: הִיא שְׂמֵחָה כִּי הִיא קִבְּלָה מַתָּנָה.
items.en: She is happy because she got a present.
items.translit: Hi smecha ki hi kibla matana.

items.en: This is the book I bought yesterday.
The man who lives here is a doctor.
I think that he is right.
She said that she would come.
Where is the car you bought? (to a man)
I have a friend who speaks Russian.
The town where I was born is small.
I know that it's hard. (woman)
Yesterday I talked with mom.
On Shabbat we visited grandma.
He is looking for a new job.
Who paid for the food?
She is telling the children a story.
I want to visit Jerusalem.
The house needs cleaning.
The teacher teaches Hebrew.
I get dressed quickly in the morning.
She called me yesterday.
They got married in the summer.
I need to wash.
The film is starting, we are excited.
I miss my family.
Call me when you arrive. (to a man)
The players train every morning.
I don't feel well.
My head hurts.
I've had a fever since yesterday.
My stomach hurts.

items.he: קַח אֶת הַתְּרוּפָה שָׁלוֹשׁ פְּעָמִים בַּיּוֹם.
items.en: Take the medicine three times a day.
items.translit: Kach et ha-trufa shalosh pe'amim ba-yom.

items.en: You need to rest.

items.he: יֵשׁ לִי תּוֹר לָרוֹפְאָה בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי.
items.en: I have an appointment with the doctor on Monday.
items.translit: Yesh li tor la-rof'a be-yom sheni.

items.en: Get well soon!
I'm looking for a dress for a wedding.
Can I try on the trousers?
Is there a bigger size?
This shirt is small on me.
That looks nice on you! (to a woman)
How much are the shoes?
Is there a discount today?
I'll buy this one.
We are looking for a flat in Tel Aviv.
How much is the rent?
The flat has a big balcony.
The kitchen is small but pleasant.
Can we see the flat tomorrow?
The flat is on the third floor.
Is there a lift in the building?
Our neighbours are nice.
Hello, who's speaking?
David speaking.
Can I speak with Rut?
She isn't home right now.
I'll call later.
I can't hear you well. (to a man)
Leave a message, please. (to a man)
I sent you a message. (to a man)
I'm happy to see you.
She is sad today.
Why are you angry? (to a man)
The boy is afraid of dogs.
I feel much better. (woman)
We're worried about you. (to a man)
He is proud of his daughter.
I'm bored.

items.he: בְּיוֹם שִׁשִּׁי בָּעֶרֶב אוֹכְלִים אֲרוּחַת שַׁבָּת.
items.en: On Friday evening people eat a Shabbat dinner.
items.translit: Be-yom shishi ba-erev ochlim aruchat shabat.

items.en: At Passover people eat matzah.
At Hanukkah people light candles.
Happy holiday to the whole family!
At Rosh Hashanah people eat apple with honey.
The shops are closed on Shabbat.
At Purim the children dress up.
A good and sweet year!
Excuse me, where is the train station?
Go straight as far as the traffic light. (to a man)
Turn right at the corner. (to a man)
The bank is opposite the post office.
Is it far from here?
It's about ten minutes on foot.
The hotel is next to the sea.
Thanks a lot, you helped me a lot. (to a man)
I always drink coffee in the morning.
She usually goes by bus.
Sometimes we eat at a restaurant.
I've never been to Eilat.
He runs once a week.
Nobody came.

items.he: כָּל יוֹם אֲנִי לוֹמֵד מִלִּים חֲדָשׁוֹת.
items.en: Every day I learn new words.
items.translit: Kol yom ani lomed milim chadashot.

items.he: הֵם כִּמְעַט אַף פַּעַם לֹא בַּבַּיִת.
items.en: They're hardly ever at home.
items.translit: Hem kim'at af pa'am lo ba-bayit.

items.en: No smoking here.
May I come in?
You should learn Hebrew. (to a man)
You can't park here.
I must go now. (woman)
Better not to drive at eight o'clock.
The children mustn't swim alone.
It's worth booking a table in advance.

lessons.title: Reading: A Trip to Eilat
lessons.context: Rut plans a holiday in the south.

paragraphs.he: בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַבָּא רוּת תִּסַּע לְאֵילַת עִם הַחֲבֵרוֹת שֶׁלָּהּ.
paragraphs.en: Next month Rut will travel to Eilat with her friends.

paragraphs.he: הֵן יִסְּעוּ בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס, כִּי זֶה יוֹתֵר זוֹל מִמָּטוֹס.
paragraphs.en: They will go by bus, because it's cheaper than a plane.
In Eilat it's always hot, even in winter.

paragraphs.he: רוּת רוֹצָה לִצְלֹל וְלִרְאוֹת דָּגִים יָפִים.
paragraphs.en: Rut wants to dive and see beautiful fish.

paragraphs.he: אִם יִהְיֶה לָהֶן זְמַן, הֵן יְבַקְּרוּ גַּם בַּמִּדְבָּר.
paragraphs.en: If they have time, they will also visit the desert.

paragraphs.he: רוּת אוֹמֶרֶת שֶׁזֶּה יִהְיֶה הַטִּיּוּל הֲכִי טוֹב שֶׁלָּהּ.
paragraphs.en: Rut says it will be her best trip.

questions.question: How will they travel to Eilat?
Why did they choose that way?
What does Rut want to see?
What will they visit if they have time?

a2-future.title: The Future Tense
a2-future.pattern: אֶלְמַד · תִּלְמַד · יִלְמַד · תִּלְמַד · נִלְמַד · יִלְמְדוּ
a2-future.explanation: The future tense is built with prefixes: אֶ־ (I), תִּ־ (you, m; she), יִ־ (he), נִ־ (we), and יִ…וּ (they). From ל־מ־ד: אֶלְמַד (I will study), תִּלְמַד (you will study / she will study), יִלְמַד (he will study), נִלְמַד (we will study), יִלְמְדוּ (they will study). 'You' to a woman adds ־ִי: תִּלְמְדִי.
a2-future.fact: In everyday speech the future is also used for polite requests: תִּסְגֹּר אֶת הַדֶּלֶת = 'close the door, would you'.

dialogue.en: When will you finish?
I'll finish in an hour.

a2-future-irr.title: Will Go, Will Come, Will Be
a2-future-irr.explanation: The most common verbs have short future forms that are worth memorising: אֵלֵךְ (I'll go), תֵּלֵךְ, יֵלֵךְ, נֵלֵךְ; אָבוֹא (I'll come), יָבוֹא, נָבוֹא; אֶהְיֶה (I'll be), יִהְיֶה (he/it will be), תִּהְיֶה (she will be), נִהְיֶה; אֶעֱשֶׂה (I'll do), נַעֲשֶׂה (we'll do).
a2-future-irr.fact: יִהְיֶה בְּסֵדֶר ('it will be fine') is probably the most Israeli sentence there is.

dialogue.en: Will you come to the party?
Yes, I'll come after work.

a2-imperative.title: Come Here! Commands and Requests
a2-imperative.pattern: בּוֹא · בּוֹאִי · שֵׁב · תֵּן לִי · אַל + future = don't
a2-imperative.explanation: Short commands: בּוֹא / בּוֹאִי / בּוֹאוּ (come, to m / f / pl), שֵׁב / שְׁבִי (sit), תֵּן / תְּנִי (give), תַּגִּיד (tell, said politely with the future). 'Don't' is אַל + the future: אַל תִּדְאַג ('don't worry'), אַל תְּדַבֵּר ('don't talk'). Add בְּבַקָּשָׁה and it's polite.
a2-imperative.fact: The future used as a command (תַּגִּיד, תָּבוֹא) sounds softer than the real imperative, so it is what most Israelis actually say.

dialogue.en: Come, sit with us!
Thanks, but don't wait for me.

a2-conj.title: Because, When, If
a2-conj.explanation: Join two ideas with: כִּי ('because'), כְּשֶׁ ('when', written joined to the next word: כְּשֶׁאֲנִי), אִם ('if'), אֲבָל ('but'), אָז ('so, then'). With אִם and כְּשֶׁ about the future, Hebrew uses the future tense in both parts: אִם יִהְיֶה חַם, נֵלֵךְ לַיָּם ('if it's hot, we'll go to the sea').
a2-conj.fact: Hebrew has no separate subjunctive: אִם + future does all the work of English 'if… will'.

dialogue.en: Why aren't you coming?
Because I'm tired.

a2-she.title: The Book That I Bought: שֶׁ
a2-she.explanation: 'That / who / which' is the prefix שֶׁ, joined to the next word: הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁקָּנִיתִי ('the book that I bought'), הָאִישׁ שֶׁגָּר פֹּה ('the man who lives here'). It also introduces what someone says or thinks: הוּא אוֹמֵר שֶׁהוּא עָיֵף ('he says that he is tired').
a2-she.fact: In formal writing you'll also see אֲשֶׁר instead of שֶׁ; it means exactly the same.

dialogue.en: Who is the woman standing there?
That's my teacher.

a2-piel.title: Piel Verbs: מְדַבֵּר, דִּבַּרְתִּי
a2-piel.pattern: present מְדַבֵּר · past דִּבַּרְתִּי · infinitive לְדַבֵּר
a2-piel.explanation: Verbs in the pattern called piel have a doubled middle letter and an 'i–e' past: דִּבֵּר (he spoke), בִּקֵּר (he visited), חִפֵּשׂ (he looked for), שִׁלֵּם (he paid). The present starts with מְ: מְדַבֵּר, מְבַקֵּר, מְחַפֵּשׂ. The infinitive starts with לְ: לְדַבֵּר, לְבַקֵּר, לְשַׁלֵּם.
a2-piel.fact: Once you hear the מְ…ֵ sound in the present (מְדַבֵּר, מְסַפֵּר, מְנַקֶּה) you can recognise piel verbs anywhere.

dialogue.en: What are you looking for?
I'm looking for the keys.

a2-hitpael.title: Hitpael: Doing It to Yourself
a2-hitpael.explanation: The pattern hitpael often means doing something to yourself or with each other. It starts with מִתְ in the present, הִתְ in the past and lehit- in the infinitive: מִתְלַבֵּשׁ (gets dressed), הִתְרַחַצְתִּי (I washed), לְהִתְקַשֵּׁר (to call), הִתְחַתְּנוּ (they got married).
a2-hitpael.fact: לְהִתְקַשֵּׁר ('to call') literally means 'to connect yourself': you 'connect yourself to' someone, אֲנִי מִתְקַשֵּׁר אֵלֶיךָ.

dialogue.en: Will you call me tomorrow?
Sure, I'll call in the morning.

a2-doctor.title: At the Doctor
a2-doctor.pattern: כּוֹאֵב לִי · יֵשׁ לִי חֹם · אֲנִי מַרְגִּישׁ לֹא טוֹב
a2-doctor.explanation: Say what hurts with כּוֹאֵב לִי + the body part: כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ ('my head hurts'); with a feminine or plural part, כּוֹאֶבֶת / כּוֹאֲבוֹת. 'I have a fever' is יֵשׁ לִי חֹם. The doctor may ask מָה מַרְגִּישׁ? or מָה כּוֹאֵב?
a2-doctor.fact: In Israel you register with a קֻפַּת חוֹלִים ('sick fund'), a health organisation that runs the clinics and covers your doctor visits.

dialogue.en: What hurts?

dialogue.native: כּוֹאֵב לִי הַגָּרוֹן וְיֵשׁ לִי חֹם.
dialogue.en: My throat hurts and I have a fever.

a2-clothes.title: Buying Clothes
a2-clothes.explanation: In a clothes shop: מָה הַמִּדָּה שֶׁלְּךָ? ('what's your size?'), אֶפְשָׁר לִמְדֹּד? ('can I try it on?'). Say how it fits with עָלַי ('on me'): זֶה קָטָן עָלַי ('it's small on me'), זֶה יָפֶה עָלַיִךְ ('it looks nice on you', to a woman).
a2-clothes.fact: End-of-season sales are called סוֹף עוֹנָה ('end of season'), and the big ones come in January and August.

dialogue.en: Can I try on the shirt?
Yes, the fitting room is there.

a2-apartment.title: Renting an Apartment
a2-apartment.explanation: Israeli flats are counted by rooms including the living room: a דִּירַת שְׁלוֹשָׁה חֲדָרִים has two bedrooms and a salon. Rent is שְׂכַר דִּירָה, the landlord is בַּעַל הַבַּיִת, and a balcony is מִרְפֶּסֶת. Most flats have a מַמָּ"ד, a reinforced safe room.
a2-apartment.fact: Many Israeli flats have a שֶׁמֶשׁ־boiler on the roof: a solar water heater, required on new buildings since the 1980s.

dialogue.en: How many rooms does the flat have?
Three rooms and a balcony.

a2-phone.title: On the Phone
a2-phone.pattern: הַלּוֹ · מִי מְדַבֵּר? · אֶפְשָׁר לְדַבֵּר עִם…?
a2-phone.explanation: Phone calls start with הַלּוֹ? or כֵּן? Ask for someone with אֶפְשָׁר לְדַבֵּר עִם…? and say who you are with מְדַבֵּר / מְדַבֶּרֶת + your name ('X speaking'). If the line is bad: לֹא שׁוֹמְעִים ('I can't hear'). End with יַאלְלָה בַּי or simply בַּי.
a2-phone.fact: Israelis often finish calls with the English 'bye' — or 'yalla bye', a mix of Arabic and English.

dialogue.en: Hello, who's speaking?

dialogue.native: מְדַבֶּרֶת דָּנָה. אֶפְשָׁר לְדַבֵּר עִם יוֹסִי?
dialogue.en: It's Dana. Can I speak to Yosi?

a2-feelings.title: How Do You Feel?
a2-feelings.pattern: אֲנִי מַרְגִּישׁ… · שָׂמֵחַ · עָצוּב · כּוֹעֵס · מְפַחֵד
a2-feelings.explanation: Talk about feelings with אֲנִי מַרְגִּישׁ / מַרְגִּישָׁה + an adjective, or just the adjective: אֲנִי עָצוּב ('I'm sad'). Feeling words agree in gender: שָׂמֵחַ / שְׂמֵחָה (happy), עָצוּב / עֲצוּבָה (sad), כּוֹעֵס / כּוֹעֶסֶת (angry), עָיֵף / עֲיֵפָה (tired). 'Afraid of' is מְפַחֵד מִ…
a2-feelings.fact: To say 'I'm bored' Hebrew uses the dative: מְשַׁעֲמֵם לִי, literally 'it's boring to me'.

dialogue.en: Why are you sad?
Because my friend is leaving.

a2-holidays.title: Holidays and Shabbat
a2-holidays.pattern: שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם · חַג שָׂמֵחַ · שָׁנָה טוֹבָה
a2-holidays.explanation: Each occasion has its greeting: שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם on Friday and Saturday, חַג שָׂמֵחַ ('happy holiday') for any festival, שָׁנָה טוֹבָה at the new year (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה), and חַג פֶּסַח שָׂמֵחַ at Passover. On Shabbat many shops close from Friday afternoon until Saturday night.
a2-holidays.fact: On Yom Kippur Israeli roads are almost empty of cars, and children ride bikes down the middle of the highways.

dialogue.en: Shabbat shalom!

dialogue.native: שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם! מָה אַתֶּם עוֹשִׂים בַּשַּׁבָּת?
dialogue.en: Shabbat shalom! What are you doing on Shabbat?

a2-directions.title: Asking the Way
a2-directions.pattern: יָשָׁר · לְיָמִין · לִשְׂמֹאל · בַּפִּנָּה · עַד הָרַמְזוֹר
a2-directions.explanation: Directions: תֵּלֵךְ יָשָׁר ('go straight'), תִּפְנֶה לְיָמִין / לִשְׂמֹאל ('turn right / left'), עַד הָרַמְזוֹר ('as far as the traffic light'), בַּפִּנָּה ('on the corner'), מוּל ('opposite'), לְיַד ('next to'). Directions are given with the future tense used as a polite command.
a2-directions.fact: Israelis are famously happy to give directions — sometimes even when they aren't sure of the way.

dialogue.en: Excuse me, where is the post office?
Go straight and turn left at the lights.

a2-frequency.title: Always, Sometimes, Never
a2-frequency.pattern: תָּמִיד · בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל · לִפְעָמִים · אַף פַּעַם לֹא
a2-frequency.explanation: How often: תָּמִיד (always), בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל (usually), לִפְעָמִים (sometimes), כִּמְעַט אַף פַּעַם (hardly ever), אַף פַּעַם לֹא (never — note the לֹא: אַף פַּעַם לֹא הָיִיתִי שָׁם, 'I've never been there'). Also כָּל יוֹם (every day), פַּעַם בְּשָׁבוּעַ (once a week).
a2-frequency.fact: Hebrew needs the double negative: אַף אֶחָד לֹא בָּא is literally 'nobody didn't come', and it's correct.

dialogue.en: Do you go to the gym?

dialogue.native: לִפְעָמִים. בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל אֲנִי רָץ לְיַד הַיָּם.
dialogue.en: Sometimes. Usually I run by the sea.

a2-modal.title: Allowed, Forbidden, Worth It
a2-modal.explanation: These words never change form and are followed by an infinitive: מֻתָּר ('it's allowed'), אָסוּר ('it's forbidden'), כְּדַאי ('it's worth it, you should'), אִי אֶפְשָׁר ('it's impossible'). Add לְ + a person to make it personal: אָסוּר לְךָ ('you mustn't'), כְּדַאי לָכֶם ('you should'). 'Must' is חַיָּב / חַיֶּבֶת, which does agree.
a2-modal.fact: You will see אָסוּר לְעַשֵּׁן ('no smoking') on signs everywhere, and לֹא כְּדַאי ('better not') in every Israeli's advice.

dialogue.en: Is it allowed to take photos here?

dialogue.native: לֹא, אָסוּר. אֲבָל כְּדַאי לִרְאוֹת אֶת הַגַּן.
dialogue.en: No, it's forbidden. But the garden is worth seeing.
